short: The Mongol state in Persia, which converted to Islam and produced a golden age of history writing.
full:
Founded by Hulagu in 1256, the Ilkhanate ruled Iran, Iraq, the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia from summer capitals at Tabriz and Maragheh. Its name means the subordinate khanate, an acknowledgement of the great khan in the east that grew emptier as the century went on. Hemmed in by the Mamluks in Syria and the Golden Horde in the Caucasus, the ilkhans sent embassies to Rome, Paris and London proposing a joint attack on Egypt; nothing came of them.

The rulers were shamanists and Buddhists who favoured Christians and Jews until Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295, after which the state became emphatically Muslim and its administration recognisably Persian. Ghazan's vizier Rashid al-Din wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, arguably the first attempt at a history of the world, drawing on Mongol, Chinese and Frankish informants. Direct Mongol rule reached Iran's astronomers, painters and tax rolls alike. Abu Sa'id died without an heir in 1335 and the state dissolved within a few years into competing successor dynasties.
